title: Health-seeking behaviour and treatment preferences among women reporting symptoms suggestive of female genital schistosomiasis in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa: A facility-based cross-sectional study
content:
by Sinegugu Shongwe, Chester Kalinda, Khumbulani Hlongwana, Themba Ginindza

Female Genital Schistosomiasis (FGS), a neglected manifestation of Schistosoma haematobium infection, affects 20–56 million women in sub-Saharan Africa and is associated with elevated HIV risk. In a Schistosoma haematobium-endemic area of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, 32% of girls aged 10–12 years reported a history of genital symptoms, yet awareness is low, and the proportion seeking appropriate care is undocumented. This study quantified healthcare-seeking behaviour and treatment preferences for FGS-suggestive symptoms across biomedical, traditional, and combined care pathways. A facility-based cross-sectional survey was conducted at eight primary healthcare clinics in iLembe District between June and August 2025, using REDCap. Of 713 women surveyed, 694 were included, and the analyses focused on 318 who reported at least one symptom suggestive of FGS, without microbiological, serological, or gynaecological confirmation. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of healthcare-seeking; among all symptomatic women, treatment preference was examined across biomedical-only, traditional/CAM-only, and combination pathways, with logistic models identifying predictors of preferring any traditional/CAM care. Analyses used Stata/SE 19. Mean age was 30.6 years (SD 8.0). Of the 318 women, 78.3% preferred only biomedical care. Women in informal employment had 4.12 times the odds of preferring traditional/CAM care compared with unemployed women (aOR = 4.12; 95% CI: 2.35–7.23; p < 0.001). In the multinomial analysis, informal employment was most strongly associated with preferring traditional/CAM care alone, carrying nearly nine times the relative risk relative to biomedical care (RRR = 8.89; 95% CI: 2.74–28.90; p < 0.001), whereas water-contact activity other than bathing was associated with a preference for combination care (RRR = 3.28; 95% CI: 1.44–7.47; p = 0.005). These findings support policies that integrate FGS screening and referral into primary healthcare, sexual and reproductive health, HIV, and antenatal services, as well as health worker training, community awareness, and coordinated referral pathways.
